title: Octane rating
description: Standard measure of the performance of an engine or aviation fuel
wiki_lead:
An octane rating, or octane number, is a standard measure of a fuel's ability to withstand compression in an internal combustion engine without causing engine knocking. The higher the octane number, the more compression the fuel can withstand before auto-igniting. The term refers to the equivalent ratio of a blend of iso-octane and heptane that produces the same knocking characteristics. Octane rating does not relate directly to the power output or the energy content of the fuel per unit mass or volume, but simply indicates the resistance to auto-ignition under pressure without a spark.
Whether a higher octane fuel improves or impairs an engine's performance depends on the design of the engine. In broad terms, fuels with a higher octane rating are used in higher-compression gasoline engines, which may yield higher power for these engines. The added power in such cases comes from the way the engine is designed to compress the air/fuel mixture, and not directly from the rating of the gasoline.
In contrast, fuels with lower octane (but higher cetane numbers) are ideal for diesel engines because diesel engines (also called compression-ignition engines) do not compress the fuel, but rather compress only air, and then inject fuel into the air that was heated by compression. Gasoline engines rely on ignition of compressed air and fuel mixture, which is ignited only near the end of the compression stroke by electric spark plugs. Therefore, being able to compress the air/fuel mixture without causing detonation is important mainly for gasoline engines. Using gasoline with lower octane than an engine is built for may cause engine knocking and/or pre-ignition.
The octane rating of aviation gasoline was extremely important in determining aero engine performance in the aircraft of World War II. The octane rating affected not only the performance of the gasoline, but also its versatility; the higher octane fuel allowed a wider range of lean to rich operating conditions.

Principles


Knocking

In spark ignition internal combustion engines, knocking (also knock, detonation, spark knock, pinging, or pinking) occurs when combustion of some of the air/fuel mixture in the cylinder does not result from propagation of the flame front ignited by the spark plug, but when one or more pockets of air/fuel mixture explode outside the envelope of the normal combustion front. The fuel-air charge is meant to be ignited by the spark plug only, and at a precise point in the piston's stroke. Knock occurs when the peak of the combustion process no longer occurs at the optimum moment for the four-stroke cycle. In a simple explanation, the forward moving wave of combustion that burns the hydrocarbon + oxygen mixture inside the cylinder like a wave that a surfer would wish to surf upon is violently disrupted by a secondary wave that has started elsewhere. grok_lead: The octane rating is a standard measure of a fuel's resistance to auto-ignition under compression in spark-ignition internal combustion engines, indicating its stability and ability to prevent knocking or pinging during combustion. This rating is crucial for gasoline, where higher values denote fuels that can endure greater compression ratios without premature detonation, allowing for more efficient engine performance. In the United States, the octane rating displayed at pumps is the Anti-Knock Index (AKI), calculated as the average of the Research Octane Number (RON) and Motor Octane Number (MON), with common grades including regular (87 AKI), midgrade (89â90 AKI), and premium (91â94 AKI). The RON is determined using a standardized test engine operating at low speed and temperature to simulate mild driving conditions, while the MON uses higher speed and temperature to mimic more severe loads, providing a comprehensive assessment of fuel performance. These numbers are established by comparing the fuel's knock intensity to reference blends of iso-octane (rated 100 for perfect resistance) and n-heptane (rated 0 for high knock tendency), as defined in ASTM International standards. Octane ratings vary globally; for instance, many countries report only RON, where values like 95 or 98 are common for premium fuels. Engine knocking, caused by uncontrolled combustion, can damage pistons and valves if not mitigated, making appropriate octane selection essential for vehicle longevity and efficiency. Modern engines often incorporate knock sensors and electronic controls to adjust ignition timing, reducing the need for higher-octane fuels in some cases, though high-compression designs like those in performance or turbocharged vehicles require premium grades to optimize power output. Factors influencing octane needs include compression ratio, ignition timing, and ambient conditions, with ethanol blends commonly boosting ratings due to their inherent high octane properties. Historically, octane enhancement began in the 1920s with tetraethyl lead additives discovered by General Motors researchers, which dramatically increased ratings but were phased out from 1973 to 1996 by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency due to severe health and environmental risks. Ethanol emerged as a lead replacement, with its use dating back to early 20th-century engines like Henry Ford's Model T, and today it constitutes about 10% of U.S. gasoline (E10 blends), providing an octane boost while reducing emissions. Other oxygenates and aromatics have also played roles in maintaining octane levels amid regulatory shifts away from toxic additives.
